entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 5 1Co 5:1-13 . The Incestuous Person at Corinth: The Corinthians Reproved for Connivance, and Warned to Purge Out the Bad Leaven. Qualification of His Former Command as to Association with Sinners of the World. 1. commonly-- rather, "actually" [Alford]. Absolutely [Bengel]. "It is reported," implies, that the Corinthians, though they "wrote" ( 1Co 7:1 ) to Paul on other points, gave him no information on those things which bore against themselves. These latter matters reached the apostle indirectly ( 1Co 1:11 ). so much as named-- The oldest manuscripts and authorities omit "named": "Fornication of such a gross kind as (exists) not even among the heathen, so that one (of you) hath (in concubinage) his father's wife," that is, his stepmother, while his father is still alive ( 2Co 7:12 ; compare Le 18:8 ). She was perhaps a heathen, for which reason he does not direct his rebuke against her (compare 1Co 5:12 , 13 ). Alford thinks "have" means have in marriage: but the connection is called "fornication," and neither Christian nor Gentile law would have sanctioned such a marriage, however Corinth's notorious profligacy might wink at the concubinage.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16829"/><div sID="gen33176" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16829"/><hi type="bold">2. puffed up--</hi>with your own wisdom and knowledge, and the eloquence of your favorite teachers: at a time when ye ought to be "mourning" at the scandal caused to religion by the incest. Paul mourned because they did not mourn (<reference osisRef="2Cor.2.4">2Co 2:4</reference>). We ought to mourn over the transgressions of others, and repent of our own (<reference osisRef="2Cor.12.21">2Co 12:21</reference>) [Bengel].<div eID="gen33176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33177" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that--</hi>ye have not felt such mourning as would lead to the result that, &c.<div eID="gen33177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33178" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">taken away from among you--</hi>by excommunication. The incestuous person was hereby brought to bitter repentance, in the interval between the sending of the first and second Epistles (<reference osisRef="2Cor.2.5-2Cor.2.10">2Co 2:5-10</reference>). Excommunication in the Christian Church corresponded to that in the Jewish synagogue, in there being a lighter and heavier form: the latter an utter separation from church fellowship and the Lord's house, the former exclusion from the Lord's Supper only but not from the Church. <div eID="gen33178" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16831"/><div sID="gen33182" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16831"/><hi type="bold">4. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ--</hi>By His authority and as representing His person and will (<reference osisRef="2Cor.2.10">2Co 2:10</reference>). Join this with "to deliver such a one unto Satan" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.5.5">1Co 5:5</reference>). The clause, "When ye have been gathered together and my spirit (wherein I am 'present,' though 'absent in body,' <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.3">1Co 5:3</reference>), with the power of our Lord Jesus," stands in a parenthesis between. Paul speaking of himself uses the word "spirit"; of Christ, "power." Christ's power was promised to be present with His Church "gathered together in His name" (<reference osisRef="Matt.18.18-Matt.18.20">Mt 18:18-20</reference>): and here Paul by inspiration gives a special promise of his apostolic spirit, which in such cases was guided by the Holy Spirit, ratifying their decree passed according to his judgment ("I have judged," <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.3">1Co 5:3</reference>), as though he were present in person (<reference osisRef="John.20.21-John.20.23">Joh 20:21-23</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.13.3-2Cor.13.10">2Co 13:3-10</reference>). This power of infallible judgment was limited to the apostles; for they alone had the power of working miracles as their credentials to attest their infallibility. Their successors, to establish their claim to the latter, must produce the former (<reference osisRef="2Cor.12.2">2Co 12:2</reference>). Even the apostles in ordinary cases, and where not specially and consciously inspired, were fallible (<reference osisRef="Acts.8.13">Ac 8:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.8.23">23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.2.11-Gal.2.14">Ga 2:11-14</reference>). <div eID="gen33182" type="x-p"/>

Their successors, to establish their claim to the latter, must produce the former ( 2Co 12:2 ). Even the apostles in ordinary cases, and where not specially and consciously inspired, were fallible ( Ac 8:13 , 23 ; Ga 2:11-14 ).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16832"/><div sID="gen33183" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16832"/>5. Besides excommunication (of which the Corinthians themselves had the power), Paul delegates here to the Corinthian Church his own special power as an apostle, of inflicting corporeal disease or death in punishment for sin ("to deliver to Satan such an one," that is, so heinous a sinner). For instances of this power, see Ac 5:1-11; 13:11; <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.20">1Ti 1:20</reference>. As Satan receives power at times to try the godly, as Job (<reference osisRef="Job.2.4-Job.2.7">Job 2:4-7</reference>) and Paul (<reference osisRef="2Cor.12.7">2Co 12:7</reference>; compare also as to Peter, <reference osisRef="Luke.22.31">Lu 22:31</reference>), much more the ungodly. Satan, the "accuser of the brethren" (<reference osisRef="Rev.12.10">Re 12:10</reference>) and the "adversary" (<reference osisRef="1Pet.5.8">1Pe 5:8</reference>), demands the sinner for punishment on account of sin (<reference osisRef="Zech.3.1">Zec 3:1</reference>). When God lets Satan have his way, He is said to "deliver the sinner unto Satan" (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.109.6">Psa 109:6</reference>). Here it is not finally; but for the affliction of the body with disease, and even death (<reference osisRef="1Cor.11.30">1Co 11:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.32">32</reference>), so as to destroy fleshly lust. He does not say, "for the destruction of the body," for it shall share in redemption (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.23">Ro 8:23</reference>); but of the corrupt "flesh" which "cannot inherit the kingdom of God," and the lusts of which had prompted this offender to incest (<reference osisRef="Rom.7.5">Ro 7:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.8.9">8:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.10">10</reference>). The "destruction of the flesh" answers to "mortify the deeds of the body" (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.13">Ro 8:13</reference>), only that the latter is done by one's self, the former is effected by chastisement from God (compare <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.6">1Pe 4:6</reference>):<div eID="gen33183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33184" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the spirit ... saved--</hi>the spiritual part of man, in the believer the organ of the Holy Spirit. Temporary affliction often leads to permanent salvation (<reference osisRef="Ps.83.16">Psa 83:16</reference>). <div eID="gen33184" type="x-p"/>

For instances of this power, see Ac 5:1-11; 13:11; 1Ti 1:20 . Temporary affliction often leads to permanent salvation ( Psa 83:16 ).

Your glorying in your own attainments and those of your favorite teachers (<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.21">1Co 3:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.19">4:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.2">5:2</reference>), while all the while ye connive at such a scandal, is quite unseemly.<div eID="gen33185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33186" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a little leaven leaveth ... whole lump--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Gal.5.9">Ga 5:9</reference>), namely, with present complicity in the guilt, and the danger of future contagion (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.33">1Co 15:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.17">2Ti 2:17</reference>). <div eID="gen33186" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16834"/><div sID="gen33187" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16834"/><hi type="bold">7. old leaven--</hi>The remnant of the "old" (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.22-Eph.4.24">Ep 4:22-24</reference>) heathenish and natural corruption. The image is taken from the extreme care of the Jews in searching every corner of their houses, and "purging out" every particle of leaven from the time of killing the lamb before the Passover (<reference osisRef="Deut.16.3">De 16:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.16.4">4</reference>). So Christians are continually to search and purify their hearts (<reference osisRef="Ps.139.23">Psa 139:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.139.24">24</reference>).<div eID="gen33187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33188" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as ye are unleavened--</hi>normally, and as far as your Christian calling is concerned: free from the leaven of sin and death (<reference osisRef="1Cor.6.11">1Co 6:11</reference>). Paul often grounds exhortations on the assumption of Christian professors' normal state as realized (<reference osisRef="Rom.6.3">Ro 6:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.6.4">4</reference>) [Alford]. Regarding the Corinthian Church as the Passover "unleavened lump" or mass, he entreats them to correspond in fact with this their normal state. "For Christ our Passover (Ex 12:5-11, 21-23; <reference osisRef="John.1.29">Joh 1:29</reference>) has been (English Version, "is") sacrificed for us"; that is, as the Jews began the days of unleavened bread with the slaying of the Passover lamb, so, Christ our Passover having been already slain, let there be no leaven of evil in you who are the "unleavened lump." Doubtless he alludes to the Passover which had been two or three weeks before kept by the Jewish Christians (<reference osisRef="1Cor.16.8">1Co 16:8</reference>): the Gentile Christians probably also refraining from leavened bread at the love-feasts. Thus the Jewish Passover naturally gave place to our Christian Easter. The time however, of keeping feast (metaphorical; that is, leading the Christian life of joy in Christ's finished work, compare <reference osisRef="Prov.15.15">Pr 15:15</reference>) among us Christians, corresponding to the Jewish Passover, is not limited, as the latter, to one season, but is ALL our time; for the transcendent benefits of the once-for-all completed sacrifice of our Passover Lamb extends to all the time of our lives and of this Christian dispensation; in no part of our time is the leaven of evil to be admitted.<div eID="gen33188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33189" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">For even--</hi>an additional reason, besides that in <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.6">1Co 5:6</reference>, and a more cogent one for purging out every leaven of evil; namely, that Christ has been already sacrificed, whereas the old leaven is yet unremoved, which ought to have been long ago purged out. <div eID="gen33189" type="x-p"/>

Paul often grounds exhortations on the assumption of Christian professors' normal state as realized ( Ro 6:3 , 4 ) [Alford]. Regarding the Corinthian Church as the Passover "unleavened lump" or mass, he entreats them to correspond in fact with this their normal state. "For Christ our Passover (Ex 12:5-11, 21-23; Joh 1:29 ) has been (English Version, "is") sacrificed for us"; that is, as the Jews began the days of unleavened bread with the slaying of the Passover lamb, so, Christ our Passover having been already slain, let there be no leaven of evil in you who are the "unleavened lump." Doubtless he alludes to the Passover which had been two or three weeks before kept by the Jewish Christians ( 1Co 16:8 ): the Gentile Christians probably also refraining from leavened bread at the love-feasts. Thus the Jewish Passover naturally gave place to our Christian Easter. The time however, of keeping feast (metaphorical; that is, leading the Christian life of joy in Christ's finished work, compare Pr 15:15 ) among us Christians, corresponding to the Jewish Passover, is not limited, as the latter, to one season, but is ALL our time; for the transcendent benefits of the once-for-all completed sacrifice of our Passover Lamb extends to all the time of our lives and of this Christian dispensation; in no part of our time is the leaven of evil to be admitted. For even-- an additional reason, besides that in 1Co 5:6 , and a more cogent one for purging out every leaven of evil; namely, that Christ has been already sacrificed, whereas the old leaven is yet unremoved, which ought to have been long ago purged out.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16836"/><div sID="gen33193" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16836"/><hi type="bold">9. I wrote ... in an epistle--</hi>rather, "in the Epistle": a former one not now extant. That Paul does not refer to the present letter is proved by the fact that no direction "not to company with fornicators" occurs in the previous part of it; also the words, "in an (or, the) epistle," could not have been added if he meant, "I have just written" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.10.10">2Co 10:10</reference>). "His letters" (plural; not applying to merely one) confirm this. <reference osisRef="2Cor.7.8">2Co 7:8</reference> also refers to our first Epistle, just as here a former letter is referred to by the same phrase. Paul probably wrote a former brief reply to inquiries of the Corinthians: our first Epistle, as it enters more fully into the same subject, has superseded the former, which the Holy Spirit did not design for the guidance of the Church in general, and which therefore has not been preserved. See my Introduction. <div eID="gen33193" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16837"/><div sID="gen33194" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16837"/>10. Limitation of the prohibition alluded to in <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.9">1Co 5:9</reference>. As in dissolute Corinth to "company with no fornicators," &c., would be almost to company with none in the (unbelieving) world; ye need not utterly ("altogether") forego intercourse with fornicators, &c., of the unbelieving world (compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.27">1Co 10:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.17.15">Joh 17:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.5.18">1Jo 5:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="1John.5.19">19</reference>). As "fornicators" sin against themselves, so "extortioners" against their neighbors, and "idolaters" against God. The attempt to get "out of the world," in violation of God's will that believers should remain in it but keep themselves from its evil, led to monasticism and its consequent evils. <div eID="gen33194" type="x-p"/>

But now--</hi>"Now" does not express time, but "the case being so," namely, that to avoid fornicators, &c., of the world, you would have to leave the world altogether, which would be absurd. So "now" is used in <reference osisRef="Heb.11.16">He 11:16</reference>. Thus we avoid making the apostle now retract a command which he had before given.<div eID="gen33195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33196" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I have written--</hi>that is, my meaning in the letter I wrote was "not to keep company," &c.<div eID="gen33196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33197" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a brother--</hi>contrasted with a "fornicator ... of the world" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.5.10">1Co 5:10</reference>). There is less danger in associating with open worldlings than with carnal professors. Here, as in <reference osisRef="Eph.5.3">Ep 5:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.5.5">5</reference>, "covetousness" is joined with "fornication": the common fount of both being "the fierce and ever fiercer longing of the creature, which has turned from God, to fill itself with the inferior objects of sense" [Trench, Greek Synonyms of the New Testament]. Hence "idolatry" is associated with them: and the covetous man is termed an "idolater" (<reference osisRef="Num.25.1">Nu 25:1</reference>, 2). The Corinthians did not fall into open idolatry, but ate things offered to idols, so making a compromise with the heathen; just as they connived at fornication. Thus this verse prepares for the precepts in <reference osisRef="1Cor.8.4">1Co 8:4</reference>, &c.
